title: Theorising research publication practices among African university-based researchers
content:
by Meshack Nzesei Mutua, Felix Otieno, Marthe Montcho, Ferdinand C. Mukumbang

Understanding research publication practices among African academics is critical to promoting knowledge equity and addressing structural and systemic challenges that disproportionately affect them, thereby increasing the quantity and quality of scientific output and catalysing socio-economic development on the continent. By exploring research publication practices among university-based African researchers, this paper offers transferable insights into how and why initiatives can promote positive publication practices, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Using an Indigenous realist evaluation approach, data were collected from three distinct African research project teams that participated in research capacity-strengthening workshops to enhance their research publication skills. Nineteen (19) interviews with the Principal Investigators and other collaborating researchers were conducted. Data analysis involved retroductive theorising, utilising the Context-Mechanism-Outcome heuristic to identify context, mechanism and outcome. We found that where early- and mid-career researchers’ career growth and promotions are based on research publications and the ‘publish or perish’ culture, providing training and financial resources for research publication would not only empower researchers but also trigger perceived pressure, resulting in improved technical skills in publication and a shift from ‘researcher-perceived quality’ to quantity of publications. When the impact factor is misconstrued as a measure of quality, and Western journals are perceived to have a ‘global’ reach, a sense of pride, prestige, and validation is triggered among African researchers, leading to increased publication in Western journals and a perceived boost in professional reputation. When African universities establish institutional ‘read and publish’ agreements with most Western journals, while African journals have low visibility and lack impact factors, perceived credibility, incentives, and trust are activated, driving African researchers to publish in Western journals and leading them to vary the perceived quality of their papers depending on the target journal. We conclude that African universities need to interrogate, with a decolonial lens, their institutional research publication and career progression policies to ensure they are responsive to their contexts.
